transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-23
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marco Liu (Redwood ML Eng); John Park (NovaScale ML Lead), Sofia Romero (Infra), Ethan Watts (SRE), Priyanka Singh (Research Eng)

Summary (auto): quick hands-on workshop to explore stochastic rounding + mixed-precision strategies to mitigate post-quantize accuracy drops; align on instruments for on-prem pilot and data to share for regression triage.

Topics: quantization modes (INT8, AWQ, GPTQ), stochastic rounding, layerwise mixed precision, KV cache impacts, batching tradeoffs, deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem.

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. quick intros — i'm alex, AE on the account.
[00:10] John: hi all, john here, i run ml at novascale. we had a pretty nasty accuracy delta after moving to int8 in our internal tests, so hoping to brainstorm mitigation.
[00:20] Priya: yeah, today we want to cover a couple approaches — stochastic rounding, mixing FP16 on sensitive layers, and AWQ/gptq variants — and then sketch bench plan for your on-prem environment.
[00:35] Sofia: small ask — also want to understand the infra implications; we run in a VPC with strict egress, hsm for keys, we can't send KV cache off-cluster.
[00:45] Alex: noted. we'll address on-prem deployment constraints later.

[01:10] Priya: jumping in — quick primer: deterministic per-tensor INT8 tends to introduce step-like quantization noise; stochastic rounding can reduce bias by randomizing rounding to nearest quant level based on residual probability. that often helps with certain prompt distributions.
[01:45] John: is stochastic rounding something we can enable at runtime or does it require model re-quant?
[01:55] Priya: depends on the quant backend. in our runtime we can enable stochastic rounding as an execution flag for AWQ-like kernels; for some GPTQ flows you have to re-quant with a different rounding scheme. we covered both paths in the doc i sent — link here: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/nova-int8-report (internal).
[02:30] Ethan: sorry, quick interject — what's the perf cost? any additional latency with stochastic rounding?
[02:40] Marco: good question — minimal on modern tensor cores if we use the stochastic RNG fused into the kernel; overhead typically 3-7% tail latency in microbenchmarks, throughput impact depends on batch sizing. but it can avoid costly re-rollouts due to accuracy regressions.

[03:20] Priya: also, mixed-precision: we often recommend keeping attention and first/last few MLP layers at FP16 and quantizing the bulk to INT8/AWQ. per-layer sensitivity varies by model family and prompt shape.
[03:50] John: when you say "attention" do you mean keys/queries/values or the whole attention block including softmax?
[03:56] Priya: generally the linear transforms (q/k/v/proj). softmax tends to be stable but the projection layers can be sensitive. there's also the interaction with KV cache — we've seen regressed completions when KV cache gets quantized too aggressively.

[04:30] Sofia: that KV cache point is huge for us. our typical use is long-context chat with prefix caching; if the KV cache is aggressive-quantized we see hallucinations after ~3k tokens.
[04:45] Priya: yeah that's a known case — our recommendation is keep KV cache in FP16 or use 16-bit mantissa-like layout (FP8 is tricky here), or apply per-kv-block quantization with higher bitwidth.
[05:05] John: are there hybrid strategies, like keep KV cache FP16 but reduce compute precision for new tokens?
[05:12] Marco: exactly. that's mixed-precision streaming: maintain FP16 KV cache, run compute through INT8/AWQ with on-the-fly dequant/quant for new KV entries. the runtime supports continuous batching with that pattern but there's serialization overhead during dequant; we can tune prefetch to hide it.

[06:00] Alex: can we surface a quick decision tree? maybe: 1) pick baseline FP16 throughput; 2) try AWQ/INT8 with stochastic rounding on sensitive prompts; 3) if regression persists, flip attention/proj to FP16; 4) if KV issues appear, pin KV to FP16.
[06:25] Priya: i sketched a short recipe in the deck — also we typically run a per-layer perturbation test to rank sensitivity: quantize one layer at a time and run your golden prompts to find delta.

[07:10] John: that per-layer test — what's the sample size we need to trust the ranking? we run thousands of prompts but can share a subset.
[07:20] Priya: recommend 200-500 prompts representative of production distribution; include edge-cases where hallucinations happened. you mentioned you'll share 200 — that should be enough to find top 10 sensitive layers.

[08:00] Sofia: infra question — if we do on-prem, we need to ensure the runtime can run inside our VPC with no egress and connect to our KMS/HSM. is that straightforward?
[08:15] Alex: yes — Redwood Private runs a control plane optionally air-gapped; for on-prem we deploy the runtime agents and you can bring-your-own-kms. we have an ops checklist: I'll share the SOW + security addendum.
[08:35] Ethan: what about kernel support? our hardware is A100 and some H100. do we need different kernels for AWQ vs INT8?
[08:45] Marco: kernel differences exist — AWQ fuses certain matrix ops differently; we auto-select kernels per-hardware. H100 introduces better int8 matmul throughput; we'll run both kernels during bench to choose the best path.

[09:20] John: can you explain AWQ vs GPTQ tradeoffs in lay terms?
[09:28] Priya: sure — GPTQ uses per-channel second-order information to minimize MSE during quant; it's great for accuracy but slower and sometimes brittle when you change seq len or attention patterns. AWQ is a newer asymmetric weight quant that aims to preserve outliers and can be faster to execute in our runtime. AWQ often gives a good speed/accuracy sweet spot.
[10:05] John: are there known failure modes where AWQ beats GPTQ or the opposite? any example?
[10:12] Priya: AWQ can outperform GPTQ when distributions have heavy-tail outliers in certain layers; GPTQ can do better if you can invest in per-layer retraining-like calibration. but both can show regressions for highly structured prompts unless you do per-layer checks.

[11:00] Priya: demo time — i pulled up a quick experiment on a small 2B-ish model (we anonymized names) to show stochastic rounding effect.
[11:10] [screen share noise, background chatter]
[11:30] Priya: here's baseline FP16 perplexity and INT8 deterministic — you can see a 4.2% delta on this prompt set. when we enable stochastic rounding the delta drops to 1.1% and subjective outputs are closer to baseline.
[11:55] John: impressive. for our workload, we care about exact token matching in a set of retrieval-augmented generation tasks — will stochastic rounding help conservatively?
[12:10] Marco: it depends. stochastic rounding reduces bias but adds variance; for RAG exact-match tasks it can help avoid systematic drift, but you'll need to run multiple seeds if your metric is sensitive to variance. usually it's worth it if deterministic int8 causes systematic errors.

[13:15] Sofia: i want to call out deterministic reproducibility — regulators in one of our verticals require deterministic outputs for audit. stochastic rounding sounds like it breaks determinism.
[13:30] Alex: good flag — we can support deterministic pseudo-stochastic via seeded RNG that is fixed per request/trace so you can have reproducible outputs across runs if needed. it's an engineering trade.

[14:05] John: what about FP8? any sweet spots?
[14:12] Priya: fp8 can be great for throughput but it's a newer format with less mature kernels; on H100 it's promising. accuracy depends heavily on exponent bias and shared ranges; often a hybrid FP8/INT8 setup is used for peak throughput. we can help pick quant profiles.

[15:00] Priya: next — batching. smaller latency-sensitive batches often favor INT8 for lower p99, but very large throughput batches benefit more from FP16 on certain kernels. prefix caching also interacts: when you have long prefix and smaller generation per request, careful KV handling is more important than raw matmul throughput.
[15:35] John: are there easy knobs in your console to experiment with batch sizes / dynamic batching thresholds?
[15:45] Alex: yes — Redwood Console exposes batch window ms, target batch size, and a mode for latency-first vs throughput-first. we'll show you the console during the pilot.

[16:20] Priya: i also want to talk about regression triage: our recommended flow is 1) reproduce locally with your prompts and our baseline; 2) run per-layer one-off quant tests and record deltas; 3) if two adjacent layers are sensitive, try flipping the earlier one to FP16; 4) if KV-only issues, pin just KV cache. we keep a short list of fallback rollouts in our producible recipes.
[17:10] John: what's the expected time to identify top-3 offending layers?
[17:20] Priya: with 200 prompts and our internal scripts it's usually a few hours on a 4-GPU rig; we'll run that off your dataset in our bench and report.

[18:05] Ethan: operationally, how much extra memory for keeping KV in FP16 vs INT8? we need to budget RAM for our GPU cluster.
[18:15] Marco: roughly 2x per-token memory for FP16 vs INT8; if you keep KV in FP16 you'll see memory usage increase which can be mitigated via selective evaporation of older prefixes or async spilling to pinned host memory.

[19:00] John: Priya, you mentioned per-layer mixed-precision recipe — can you give a quick example?
[19:08] Priya: sure — sample recipe: quantize all MLP blocks to INT8, quantize attention proj to INT8 but keep q/k/v/proj of the first 2 and last 2 layers at FP16, pin KV to FP16, enable stochastic rounding for linear kernels, and use AWQ backend for matmuls. we can tune layer indices after sensitivity ranking.

[20:00] Sofia: how do we manage rollbacks? if we deploy quantized model on-prem and see regressions in production, is there an automated fallback to FP16 model?
[20:10] Alex: yes — rollout policies in Redwood can do canary followed by automatic rollback if metric thresholds breach (we'll need to integrate your health metrics). for on-prem we run a local health agent that evaluates sample golden prompts.

[21:30] John: any gotchas with tokenization / vocab when you mix precisions?
[21:40] Priya: tokenization is orthogonal; but numerical changes can alter beam search tie-breaks. we advise keeping decoding seeds and logits temp consistent. small numeric differences may amplify in some decoder heuristics.

[22:20] Priya: lastly a note on regression bisecting: sometimes the culprit is not quantization but prompt preprocessing differences or batch shaping. when we saw odd regressions before, the top 3 causes were: 1) KV cache quantization; 2) decoder temp mismatch; 3) per-layer outlier handling. so check those early.

[23:10] Alex: ok let's recap — action items (we'll post in crm): Redwood runs targeted bench, NovaScale uploads prompts, Redwood shares mixed-precision recipe and SOW, schedule pilot kickoff.

[23:40] John: thanks everyone. quick logistics: can you send the security addendum and compliance deck?
[23:48] Alex: yes — sending SOC2 + SAML/KMS integration doc after this call.

[24:05] Priya: one more quick thing — i'll include a short script that does per-layer quant perturbation so you can reproduce locally; it's in the repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quant-tools (demo branch).
[24:25] John: perfect. looking forward to the bench.

[24:40] [wrap up chatter, scheduling ping noises]
